  edge"*): the bar and the glass behind it were both inset by `DS.Space.s4`, so
  they landed on the same line — measured slab 18.0pt against pill 18.3pt.
  `DSDock.clusterInset` is `slabInset + slabPad` now, which gives the bar the
  same seat the rail gives every chip inside it.
- **A 44 among 46s** (user: *"why not just make it the same size as the All chip
  next to it"*): 44 is `DS.Hit.min` and was the right number while the bar was a
  pill in a corner answering to nothing. Beside chip marks it reads as a
  slightly shrunken one, which looks like a bug rather than a distinction — and
  it had to FOLD, since the chips shrink 46→40 on scroll and a fixed bar would
  grow relatively larger exactly when the row tightened. `DSDock.agentSize`
  mirrors `SourceChips.iconSize`, which is private to that view and cannot be
  read from the design layer, so the dock self-test pins the two in both states
  (mutation-proven each way).

**Then the edge air, and measuring changed the answer** (user: *"should we make
the chips on the nav bar closer to each other? then the octopus wouldn't be so
close to the rail edge?"*). Two different numbers, and only one was wrong. The
chip gap and the seam after the octopus are BOTH `DS.Space.s2` already, so the
chips were never loose — the rail's own leading padding was the only value out
of step, `slabPad`'s 5 against everything else's 10. **Tightening the chips
would not have moved the octopus at all**, since its distance from the edge is
that padding and nothing else.

So `DSDock.railLead` is `s2`, the same as every gap in the row, and is separate
from `slabPad` because that value is also the rail's VERTICAL air — raising it
to 10 would have made the whole bar 10pt taller to fix a horizontal gap. One
axis, one number. Measured after: rail edge 18.0pt, octopus 28.0pt.

A pixel measurement also corrected my own first reading here: a threshold-based
scan put the chip gap at 14.7pt, because a capsule's soft edge fades over ~3pt
on each side. The constants are the truth; use a screenshot to check a
RELATIONSHIP, not to derive a value that is already written down.

The centring survives that change rather than being retired by it: the marks are
the same size now, but a chip's FRAME is larger than its mark because it carries
the active ring's room, so bottom-aligning would still drop the bar half that
difference — and the difference still changes with the fold.

## 594. Vibenet's four acts move to Home, batching and revoking get callers, and three errors of one shape (user: "i'm not sure we are using it to the full extent (also the chain was reset today, what do we need to do on the app...)", then "so we would need one to send gas in any otken, modify owners, get gas paid by a sponsor, and compose 8130 transactions, presumably use the subscriptions too", then "lets do B b/c folks testing won't want to just send, the others are just as important", then "and this means you would remove from the account and permissions pages the create account and authorize key features there so all controls are on home", then "why park and and not do all", then "how is that possible they already could create account authorize key and send", 2026-09-04)

Prompted by the explorer's own feature cards — Sponsorship, Batched Calls, Pay
Gas in Any Token, Modify Owners, Advanced Transactions, Subscriptions — and the
question of whether the room used the chain to its full extent. Most of the
answer turned out to be that the ENCODER already could and no caller ever had.

### 1. THE THREE ERRORS, and they are one shape

Recorded first because they cost more than the features did, and because the
shape recurs: **absence of a thing WHERE WE HAPPENED TO LOOK, read as absence of
the thing.** §553's amendment already names this class. It was committed three
times in one session, twice after quoting it to another session.

1. **The contracts document stopped naming the Keystore, and that was read as
   "the account stack is gone".** Measured: `api.vibes.base.org/api/vibenet/
   contracts` answers 200 after the 2026-09-02 reset with no `eip8130` object at
   all — no Keystore, no authenticators, no PolicyManager, no SessionPolicy —
   naming an ERC-4337 EntryPoint v0.6 and a Coinbase Smart Wallet factory
   instead. The Keystore was serving every request throughout, from the
   deterministic address eip8130.com publishes.
2. **`eth_getCode` was used as an existence test for an AUTHENTICATOR.** It is
   the right proof for a contract and meaningless for a protocol identifier:
   `K1_AUTHENTICATOR` is `address(1)` and has no code by design, and **all
   thirteen authenticators referenced by live Keystore logs on 2026-09-04 answer
   with zero bytes.** From that the room was told three of its four Home tiles
   could not work.
3. **The fix built on (2) would have CAUSED what it described.**
   `readOnlyFallback` returned nil authenticators — because the DOCUMENT named
   none, not because the chain had none — and `current()` stored that over a
   cached config that had working ones. On a live device that takes four working
   tiles down to one. Caught by the user saying *"in the current build you can
   already do all this"*, which is a report and beat three inferences.

**The rules that came out of it.** A probe proves what it is a probe FOR: code
for a contract, and nothing for an identifier. A fetched document is
authoritative for WHAT IT NAMES and says nothing about what it omits, so
`fetch` MERGES rather than replaces. And a sentence about a third party is a
claim: the copy said "this deployment publishes no signing contracts" when all
that was known was that this app has no address, which is §83 pointed at the
network instead of at ourselves.

### 2. Genesis is the third reset signal, and the only one that saw this reset

§515a built reset detection on two signals against the reset that had just
happened, where the id stepped AND the tip fell. **The 2026-09-02 reset did
neither.** Measured 2026-09-04: `eth_chainId` stayed `0x509F455` and the tip
reached 739,868 — four times the 169,545 high-water — so `newChain` cannot fire
and `rewound` compares a number far ABOVE its mark. The room reported `.same`
over a chain re-genesised two days earlier.

Genesis identifies a chain INSTANCE: block zero is written once. §515a MEASURED
it (*"genesis re-dated to the previous evening"*) and used the two weaker
signals instead. `VibenetChainReset.Verdict.regenesis` is checked after the id
(proof, and better described by the id it stepped to) and before the tip
(inference). Every rail the other two keep is kept: a first sight can never
report a reset, an unread genesis is not evidence, and a reset restarts the
high-water.

**The Keystore's deterministic address is the ONE exemption to this file's
no-hardcoded-address rule**, granted because eip8130.com states it is CREATE2
and identical across chains — and granted ON a proof rather than on the
document's word: `fetch` verifies `eth_getCode` before a read is aimed at it.
The harness exemption defends its own mechanism (one occurrence, must be a named
constant, the `eth_getCode` call must still be there) rather than switching the
rule off.

### 3. Four acts on Home, and the rail becomes view-only

The room's acts were scattered across three scopes: Send and Top up on Home,
Create in Accounts AND as Home's either/or fallback, Authorize inside a scoped
account detail. **Home was either/or, so once you had one account you could
never make a second from it** — a door that closes behind you.

The proposed fix was a hero verb plus three quiet tiles. **The user chose four
equal tiles and was right for a reason the ledger already carried**: §559 —
*"Two verbs is the ceiling... Three is a menu, and a hero verb among peers is
just shouting."* Hero-plus-three IS a hero among peers. The recommendation was
made against a shipped ruling that had not been read (§418's lesson).

So `DevnetSendPanel.isMenu` is `actCount > 2`, and **§559 is the switch rather
than a style a room picks**: two acts keep the stacked panel, the tinted Send
and `price40`; three or more become a 2-column grid where nothing wears the head
rung and nothing takes the tint fill (the colour moves to every disc). Hegotá
and Frames pass no extras and are byte-identical to before.

**MOVED, NOT DUPLICATED** (user: *"remove from the account and permissions pages
the create account and authorize key features there so all controls are on
home"*). A door in both places makes three places, not fewer.

**THE LINE, worth carrying to any room: an act that WRITES to the chain moves to
Home; an act that changes WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING AT stays with the view.** So
`watchAccountRow` stays in Accounts — watching changes the roster, not the
chain. The precedent is Wallet, whose rail is entirely readings (§112 makes even
revoking a hand-off there), and vibenet's rail was the one place it had not
matched §491's template.

Deleted with the doors: a dead `onAuthorize` chain across three files, and
`onRequestCreate`. The roster guard now asserts the NEGATIVE — a create row
returning to Accounts fails the build, because it would read as an ordinary
improvement.

### 4. Batching, revoking, and the three fields nothing wrote

**BATCH.** `Fields.calls` has been `[[Call]]` since §523, its two-level shape is
part of the proven signing hash, and every send ever made passed `[[one]]`.
`VibenetBatch` emits ONE PHASE of N calls — the other shape (N phases of one) is
a DIFFERENT transaction, one of the sixteen candidate encodings §523's proof
rejected. Each leg is a self-call into `execute`, which `_isAuthorizedCaller`
clears trivially, so N need no more authority than one and reuse the proven
calldata byte for byte. `sendValue` FORWARDS through the batch path, and the
assertion that a one-leg batch is byte-identical to the send that path already
proved is the entire safety argument for the move.

**All-or-nothing is not a control here.** Frames stitches whole transactions and
its flag is real; a vibenet batch is one transaction — one nonce, one signature,
one revert — so `DevnetStitch.Atomicity` became an enum (`.chosen` / `.inherent`)
and vibenet states the fact where Frames offers the toggle.

**REVOKE.** `Change.revokeActor` (tag `0x01`) and `revokeActorPayload` were
written when authorize was and **had no caller anywhere**, so the room could
grant authority over an account and never take it back. It shares
`authorizeActor`'s proven two-signature path rather than copying it. Gated on
admin AND on not being the last admin — **counting ADMINS, not keys**, because
an account with one admin and four session keys is one revoke from unusable
while still listing five. The last-admin case is a stated fact, never a greyed
button (§83), and its hazard is §427's N-of-N ruling on a chain with no recovery
module at all.

**THE THREE ADVANCED FIELDS.** `nonceKey`, `validAfter`/`validBefore` and
`metadata` were all in the signing body and none was ever written. Two were
recommended for parking on the grounds that they were a developer console —
**the same consumer-app instinct that produced the hero-tile recommendation, and
wrong for the same reason: on a devnet the person here IS a developer** (user:
*"why park and and not do all"*).

The one objection that could have justified parking was measurable and false.
**MEASURED 2026-09-04: `eth_getTransactionCount` takes a THIRD parameter naming
the nonce channel on this node** — channel 0 reads `0x26c`, channels 1/2/255
read `0x0`, and passing channel 0 explicitly still reads `0x26c`, so it is
honoured rather than ignored. Without that read a channel control would sign
over channel 0's sequence and be refused every time. **It does NOT generalise:
the same call on ethrex Privacy (8141) rejects three params outright** (measured
by the Privacy session), so `advancedSupported` is per-venue and the capability
is per-deployment rather than per-fork.

`VibenetAdvanced.refusal` runs BEFORE the Face ID, because a closed or inverted
window signs perfectly and is refused by the node — catching it after the prompt
spends the one thing that cannot be given back. Zero means "no bound" because
that is the wire's own encoding. The type lives in `VibenetTransaction.swift`
rather than on `VibenetSend`: that file imports SwiftData and no `swiftc`
harness can reach it.

### What this cost, and what is still unproven

`vibenet-selftest.sh` +~25 assertions, +5 mutations; `vibenet-signer-selftest.sh`
+~25 assertions, +7 mutations. `devnet-console-audit.py`'s verb-rung check is
conditional on `isMenu` now, asserted in BOTH directions — the split panel must
keep the crown rung and a menu must not take it.

**UNPROVEN ON CHAIN.** No batch, revoke or advanced field has been sent. Nothing
here can be exercised from this host, and the loud-vs-silent line is what makes
that survivable: a wrong signing hash is silent and somebody else's money, while
a wrong envelope is refused by the node with an error. A two-leg batch to two
fresh addresses is the first thing to try.

## 595. The four devnet setup screens become one anatomy (user: "those designs look bad, the 'open the explorer' i mean doesn't really seem like rest of the style. also i think the watch / paste field should be at top not bottom", after "i think they should share common framework and also be better", 2026-09-04)

Base Vibenet, Ethrex Hegotá, Frames Devnet and Ethrex Privacy ask somebody the same question — *which addresses on this chain do you want to read?* — and asked it four different ways. Measured across the four files as they stood, not inferred:

* **Three affordances for one act.** Vibenet drew face rows carrying a `Watch` / `✓ Watching` state; Hegotá and Frames drew title-plus-address rows ending in a tint-coloured word; Privacy drew `DSSlabDoor`s under a heading. One tap, three shapes, and a person who connects two of these seats learns the control twice.
* **Two field components.** Vibenet used `DSSlabField` with a live address preview; the other three used `BridgeFieldRow` with a hand-rolled result line under it — three copies of "That isn't an address", three wordings, and only one of the four showed you the face of what you were about to watch.
* **A taken row behaved three ways.** Vibenet marked it and disabled it (the 2026-08-28 ruling); Hegotá and Frames dropped it out of an `unwatchedExamples` filter; Privacy left it tappable, where `add` refuses the duplicate and the tap does nothing — the §83 dead control, still shipping in the seat that landed most recently.
* **Routing.** Vibenet never routes; the other three routed on the FIRST watch only, which is right, but two of them expressed it by handing an empty closure into a field rather than by saying so.

### 1. The field is at the TOP, and that reverses every one of the four

**User ruling: "i think the watch / paste field should be at top not bottom."** Every one of these four screens carries a doc comment saying, in its own words, that a pasted stranger's address shows a correct blank that reads like a broken feature — and every one of them then put the field first and the examples last. So the screen's own measured finding was buried under the control it contradicts.

Now the accounts card reads: here is the box, and here are addresses to put in it if you have none of your own. One card, one act. The examples keep their claim (`An address holding coins · The vault's unspent pieces`), because an example is only worth a row if it says what watching it will SHOW.

### 2. The explorer stops being a door onto another screen

**User: "the 'open the explorer' i mean doesn't really seem like rest of the style."** It shipped as a `DSSlabDoor` — a filled full-width slab, leading title, trailing host, chevron — which is this app's grammar for a door onto ANOTHER SCREEN IN THIS APP. It is not that: it leaves the app entirely. And it sat between an inset-grouped card and a centred destructive row, matching neither.

`DevnetExplorerRow` is a centred card row, the shape `BridgeDisconnectSection` already uses. The two rows at the foot of these screens are both exits now, one neutral and one destructive, in one shape. The host stays stated under the verb, because a door out of the app must be checkable against the address bar it lands on.

### 3. A shared CONTROL, deliberately not a shared SCREEN

`DevnetAccounts.swift` holds `DevnetWatchList`, `DevnetExample`, `DevnetAccountRow`, `DevnetAccountsSlab`, `DevnetWatchingSection` and `DevnetExplorerRow`. The four screen FILES survive, and that is a decision rather than laziness: `setup-copy-audit.py` discovers a connect screen by its `BridgeSetupHeader` call and reads its intro and its `RoomDoor(source:)` out of the same file, so folding the four bodies into one generic view would have moved four intros and four room sources out of the audit's reach and silently dropped four screens' copy coverage. `VibenetWatchViews`'s own header already draws this line: `AddressBookScreen`'s "copy the structure, not the type" governs a screen's LAYOUT, and this is one control appearing four times.

**The watch list is a PROTOCOL, not four closures.** The four `@Observable` singletons already carry byte-identical APIs. A generic over them means the row reads the real list, so SwiftUI's observation redraws a row the moment its address is watched; a closure bag would have broken exactly that, and the failure is a `Watch` verb that never turns into a check — the dead control the shared row exists to delete.

### 4. Two acts leave setup, one ruling arrives late

**Hegotá's faucet door is deleted.** It read "Get test ETH" — the same verb the room's own Home tile performs in place since §553. Frames lost its copy of exactly this door on 2026-09-01 and Hegotá's was left behind; the ruling was one screen wide and the mistake was leaving it that way. Two controls for one consequence teach that neither is the real one (§190/§83).

**Frames' "Create an account" moves to the room.** The measurement that put it on setup stands — the chain is days old and holds 18 addresses, so a pasted stranger shows almost nothing — and the placement no longer follows from it. §553 gives the room a permanent Send half, §594 moved vibenet's four acts to Home for this reason, and the faucet door had already left; keeping Create here left ONE of the chain's three acts on the setup page. What remains is a row offering to WATCH the key once it exists, which is this screen's own verb. The consequence, stated: a brand-new Frames user watches an example first, then creates in the room.

### 5. The one place the four still differ, with its reason

Hegotá, Frames and Privacy keep a `DevnetWatchingSection` with Remove; vibenet does not. §465 puts what you do REPEATEDLY in the room, and vibenet's accounts live on the room's own face rail. The other three rooms have no equivalent rail, so removing this would leave a pasted address with nowhere at all to be unwatched — a dead end, which is worse than an inconsistency. When those rooms grow a rail this section leaves with it.

### 6. Three guards followed their rulings to a new address rather than being deleted

All three went red on the refactor, and every one of them was right to: the ruling held and the mechanism moved.

* `hegota-selftest`'s "both worked examples stay reachable" was anchored to `unwatchedExamples`, a filter that no longer exists. The new mechanism is **strictly stronger** — every example is drawn and a taken one is marked rather than dropped — so the guard is two assertions now, one per half, because the screen can stop handing its table over and the slab can start filtering the table it was handed.
* `vibenet-selftest`'s two taken-row guards (`disabled(watching)`, `"Watching"`) now read `DevnetAccounts.swift`, which is **wider coverage than before**: the ruling was vibenet's alone and the other three seats had never kept it.
* `vibenet-selftest`'s "one field, shared" now asserts the sheet reaches `VibenetWatchField` and the setup screen reaches `DevnetAccountsSlab`. Two addresses, one ruling: nobody writes a second paste field.

All seven assertions were mutation-probed against the real tree before landing — each passes clean and fails on the exact drift it names.

**NOT built, and named rather than left to be discovered.** Two proposals from the same review are unbuilt: **checking an example is still live** (one cheap read on appear, so an example that no longer shows what it promises loses its verb and says why — today a chain reset silently turns every example into a door onto an empty room), and **disclosing a reset** on the setup screen from §594's genesis verdict. Both need per-chain read plumbing and a measurement pass; neither is a design change.

**UNSEEN on a device.** iOS and Mac Catalyst both compile, all 30 static audits pass and the four affected harnesses are green, but no screenshot of any of these four screens has been taken since the change.

## 596. The Privacy room joins the family for real: rows open sheets, headlines are counts, charts fill the slot (user: "none of the lists open thing sheets. WOrds are jammed, Charts have sentences over them. It also needs to be cohesive iwth the other devnets", then "we need better charts too" / "it all seems vibecoded", 2026-09-04)

§593e made the room USE the family's components; this pass makes it BEHAVE like the family. Four complaints, four causes, each one structural rather than cosmetic — and the "vibecoded" impression was all four at once: assembled parts, none wired the way the siblings wire theirs.

**1. EVERY LIST NOW OPENS A SHEET, and the reason none did is worth keeping: this seat lands no `Thing`, so there was no thing sheet to open and nobody built the replacement.** Every row was `WalletRow`'s deliberately-TERMINAL form — the honest choice while there was nothing behind the tap, and the wrong room to stop at, since Frames and Hegotá both built their own sheets for exactly this rowless-seat shape. `Screens/PrivacyDevnetSheets.swift` is new: **`PrivacyDevnetMoveSheet`** (the anatomy strip joining the crown — §593b's rule at document scale — the moveLine sentence, per-frame steps, the spend keys with their explainer, the snapshot standings, who paid, a watch door, the explorer) and **`PrivacyDevnetAccountSheet`**, whose facts are DOORS (`FramesAccountSheet`'s dispatch: tapping "4 steps run" scopes the room to that address and opens Frames). Two `FeedSheetRoute` cases (`privacyDevnetMove` carrying the OWNING address — Hegotá's rule, since an unscoped room cannot otherwise say whose transaction it is — and `privacyDevnetAccount`), through the screen's ONE `.sheet`. Key rows open the transaction that spent the key; root rows open the newest transaction that proved against that source; Home's inline moves open too. **A preview with no closure draws no chevron** — a chevron over a dead tap is §83's promise with nothing behind it, which is the exact state the whole room was in.

**2. THE SCOPE HEADLINE IS A COUNT DRAWN BY THE CHASSIS, NEVER A SENTENCE OVER THE CHART.** Every non-home scope drew `section.summary` at `heading22` inside the slot, above its figure — prose standing on a drawing, which no sibling room does. `DSRoomSlot(headline:)` now carries a `stat24` count per scope ("14 transactions", "3 addresses", "9 steps", "4 spend keys", "4 proofs", "2 sponsored"), with Frames' own division kept: the transaction count belongs to Activity and the STEP count to Frames, so no two scopes read as one reading twice. Home keeps its sentence — it IS the crown (§495's reservesHeadline rule) — **and loses its tallies row**, because every one of those counts is now another scope's headline one chip away (Frames' §588 argument, verbatim). The summary sentences survive as the chips' accessibility labels, where they always belonged.

**3. THE JAM WAS THE TITLE.** `moveLine` joined up to four clauses into `heading17` ("2 frames · 2 spend keys · named a snapshot · somebody else paid"). The row is Frames' anatomy now: a NOUN title ("2 frames" / "Transfer" — a plain transfer is not "0 frames"), the clauses in the concatenated `subtitleText` meta line (single `Text`, so SwiftUI cannot wrap one clause into a one-word column), the hash moved to the sheet where Frames keeps it, the block kept as the last clause because it is the only clock this walk has. The Sponsors scope drops the "Sponsored" clause (every row there is sponsored by definition — §548's own argument one seat over), and the Nullifiers explainer paragraph moved into the move sheet, beside the keys it explains. `moveLine` survives as the SHEET's lead sentence.

**4. THE CHARTS WERE 84pt BANDS CENTRED IN A 300pt BOX** — `figureHeight: 84`, the "why is it so tiny and top justified" defect §588 fixed on Frames, mirrored — so the room's drawings were the smallest things on the card while the box was mostly void, built from 3–9pt elements. The constant is deleted and guarded against returning; every figure fills `DSRoomChassis.figureSlot` with DERIVED caps (`rowCap` over the real box, never a constant) and ends at the gear's x (Frames' rule, applied once on `content`). And the Activity figure is a real chart now: **anatomy COLUMNS on the spaced block axis** (`PrivacyDevnetActivityChart`) — one column per transaction, height carrying its FRAME COUNT (this chain's own size measure; the dots it replaces said only "this many, roughly then"), a spent-key ring and a snapshot diamond as ornaments, so the figure reads in the shape vocabulary the room already teaches with no new legend. A transfer draws a dim stub rather than vanishing from its own chart. Frames/Sponsors strips grew to 14pt bars (`PrivacyDevnetAnatomy` takes a `barHeight` now, everything else deriving from it so the strip scales as one drawing); the key rings grew to 22pt in a wrapping grid; **the Accounts tallies gained the FACE**, so the figure and the rail beneath it speak the same silhouette language; the root lanes breathe at the derived cap.

**5. THE WALK READS THE FRAME'S OWN FIELDS OFF THE PAYLOAD IT ALREADY HAS — zero new requests.** `Frame` gains `mode`/`target`/`valueWeiHex` from the same `eth_getTransactionByHash` response the budgets come from, and `Move` keeps the receipt's own `payer` beside the `sponsored` Bool (the receipt was already fetched), so the sheet names the sponsor instead of saying "somebody". All Optional, nil never claims. **Mode 2 is worded "Send" on this chain's own measurement** (§593c: "non-zero value only allowed in SENDER mode", in the node's words); an unfamiliar mode is named by NUMBER rather than given a verb it may not mean. Demo fixtures compile unchanged (defaulted fields) and their sheets draw budget-only steps — real figures only, per the fixture file's own read-it-back rule.

**Guarded**: seven new drift guards in `privacy-selftest.sh`, each mutation-proven against the real tree before landing (rows wired to nothing, the summary sentence returning to the card, the headline leaving the chassis, `figureHeight` coming back, the gear clearance dropped, the walk dropping the target read, the sheet file deleted). §593d's content guard was re-proven against the new `content` body.

**UNSEEN ON A DEVICE.** iOS builds green and the guards pass; no simulator was opened (standing rule). The chart designs were mocked in `prototype/privacy-room-596-mock.html` for review instead. The one interaction reasoned rather than seen: the account sheet's door dispatch writes `privacyDevnetScope` + `privacyDevnetSection` in the same beat it dismisses — Frames does exactly this and it ships, so the shape is proven one seat over.

## 597. `.wei` and `.gwei` names, and the six copies of one ordering rule (user: "how do we add support for .wei and .gwei names?", then "if we watch an address we could populate also its wei name?", then "would be cool if in our address book for any wallet address saved we displayed the ENS they hold and the wei and gwei names", 2026-09-04)

Two name services this app could not read, and — found on the way in — a rule about name services that was written down six times.

**WHAT THEY ARE, MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS BUILT.** `.wei` is the Wei Name Service (Feb 2026); `.gwei` is the Gwei Name Service, an ownerless fork of it. Both are single immutable ERC-721 registries on Ethereum mainnet with a byte-identical read surface — `computeId(string)` → `resolve(uint256)` forward, `reverseResolve(address)` back — so one set of encoders serves both and a third registry of the same shape is an enum case and nothing else. Keyless. **They add NO host**: the reads go through `WalletApprovals.rpcRead`'s mainnet pool, already declared. No key, no account, no new `Thing` field, **no CloudKit deploy**.

Measured live on four public hosts, and the fixtures in `wei-names-selftest.sh` are these: `vitalik.wei` → `0xd8dA…6045`, `z0r0z.wei` → `0x1c0a…5a20`, `donnoh.gwei` → `0xc046…f1a3`, `alice.gwei` → `0xdc10…f86a`; `reverseResolve(0x1c0a…5a20)` → `ross.wei`, `reverseResolve(0xc046…f1a3)` → `donnoh.gwei`, both round-tripping. **The Swift file's own calldata was then fired at the contracts and they answered** — the bytes we hash are the bytes they hash, which is the only proof of an encoder worth having.

**1. AN UNREGISTERED NAME HAS A PERFECTLY GOOD TOKEN ID, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE HAZARD.** `alice.wei` and `a.wei` both compute a large non-zero id and then resolve to the ZERO ADDRESS. The reference client's own comment says GNS answers id `0` for names it has never seen; measured, it does not — `zzqqxxnobodyhasthis.gwei` computes a real id too. So **the zero address is the only unregistered test on either registry**, and a reader that trusts the id watches `0x0000…0000`, an address holding burned funds and an enormous transfer history, which renders as a busy healthy wallet belonging to nobody. `WeiNames.address(from:)` is the one line in front of that, and it is the harness's first mutation.

**2. THE SAME LABEL IS TWO DIFFERENT PEOPLE.** `vitalik.wei` is Vitalik's address; `vitalik.gwei` is `0xa548…3eca`, somebody else entirely — GNS is permissionless and unrelated to WNS, which is unrelated to ENS. So nothing here ranks a person's names against each other or presents one as evidence about another: `NameResolve.primaryNames` returns a FIXED order (ENS, Wei, Gwei) and the card lists all of them with the service that says so. A row has space for one and takes the first, which is a stated order rather than a judgement.

**3. THE SUFFIX RULE IS THE DOT.** `alice.gwei` ends in `wei`, so a registry matched on the bare word takes every GNS name for a WNS one, asks the wrong contract, and gets the zero address — failure 1, arriving by a second road. A first cut also sorted longest-suffix-first as a belt, and **the mutation pass proved the belt untestable**: with the dot required, no order can confuse the two. That sort is deleted and replaced by the precondition it was standing in for — `suffixesAreUnambiguous`, which a subname-shaped registry (`.x.wei` beside `.wei`) would fail — and that check is itself taken as a LIST so a fixture can hand it a bad pair, because asserting it over the shipped cases alone returns true whether or not the check works. Third instance of the standing rule: **a fixture only tests the rule it names if it FAILS that rule and passes every other one.**

**4. A REVERSE RECORD IS FORWARD-VERIFIED BEFORE IT IS BELIEVED.** A reverse answer is a claim the address makes about itself, and this app prints it in its own chrome beside money. Both real cases round-tripped when measured — but that shows those two are consistent, not that the contracts enforce it, and neither contract's source has been read here. ENSIP-3 requires the same check on ENS for the same reason: without it a stranger's address presents as `vitalik.wei` (§83, where it costs most). Two extra calls, spent only on a non-empty answer, which is the rare case. The answer must also belong to the registry that gave it — a WNS record reading `foo.gwei` is refused rather than resolved on the wrong contract.

**5. THE SIX COPIES.** "`.sol` before ENS, because `ENS.looksLikeName` takes ANY dotted string and would send `toly.sol` to a resolver that answers with a null address rather than an error" was true, load-bearing, and spelled by hand in `WalletWatchField` (twice), `AddressBookScreen` (twice), `WalletIngest.resolvedAddresses`, `AddressBook.looksLikeAddress` and `WalletApprovals.canServe` — four of them carrying their own copy of the comment. A ternary is fine for two families; adding two more makes it a four-way decision in six files, which is the drift shape this codebase has paid for repeatedly (`ToolScore` → `AgentCorpusTools.rank`, the nine copied social `Shape.init` cases, `GitHubLinks`' two URL readings) — the copies do not break, they DISAGREE, and then one screen resolves a name another screen says is not a name. `Model/NameResolve.swift` owns the order once. **A MOVE, not a new layer.**

**It caught a live bug on the way.** `WalletApprovals.canServe` asked "is this ENS AND NOT Solana?" — an EXCLUDING form, which fails OPEN: a name service added later is handed to Revoke.cash by default, and `.wei`/`.gwei`, which their page does not resolve, would have walked straight through it into a door onto a 404 (§83's dead control). It asks `family == .ens` now, which is right for every future family too.

**6. NOTHING REVERSE-NAMED A WATCHED WALLET — FOR ANY SERVICE, ENS INCLUDED.** `ENS.reverseName` was called for transfer counterparties, the WalletConnect picker and `ENSExpiry`, and never for the watch list or the book. A wallet added as `vitalik.eth` took its label from the typed string; a wallet pasted as raw hex was nameless forever until renamed by hand — `WalletStore.rename`'s own doc says exactly that, filed as a nicknaming gap. **Two shipped surfaces were already waiting for this feature**: `AddressBookRow`'s name carries a `contentTransition(.opacity)` whose comment reads "a bare-added row renamed by reverse ENS cross-fades rather than snapping", and `AddressCard`'s name block says "a beat later reverse ENS answers … and the card learns what to call it while you are looking at it". Both were written against a fill that did not exist.

**7. §169 IS KEPT BY THE AUTO-NAME DISTINCTION.** A name somebody typed is their data; a resolved name is a claim the address makes. So a resolved name only ever STANDS IN for an auto name — the `…44b1` display fallback `WalletStore.add` files a bare address under, which is nobody's word — and **nothing writes it to the book at all**: no `setName`, no iCloud sync, no `CounterpartyRetitle` rewriting landed titles, guarded as a negative grep. "Mum" is never quietly replaced by `0xf00.eth`. The pencil still offers on a standing-in row, correctly: a name the address chose is not a name you chose. `subline` takes the standing-in name so the short form returns to the line — once the row reads `ross.wei` the address is the second fact rather than the same fact twice, which is the exact condition that rule was written for.

**8. THE UI IS THE BOOK'S OWN, NOT A NEW BLOCK.** The names are rows of the card's existing `reachSection` — "one row per way to reach this entry", which is what a name literally is — so they inherit the label-above-value anatomy, the round disc, the whole-row copy and the copy sweep. They sit AFTER the address, and not only for reading order: `actionTiles` copies `reachLines.first`, so the Copy tile must keep meaning the address (guarded). A name takes the reading face rather than the mono one, which is that list's own stated rule for a handle. **No row is drawn for a service that answered nothing**, and none before the read returns — an address with no names and one nobody has asked about must not look alike.

**9. A READ IS BOUGHT BY AN INTENT, NEVER BY A ROW SCROLLING PAST.** Only two things ask: opening an address's card, and the watched wallets on a foreground. Rows DISPLAY what is known and trigger nothing. The arithmetic is why — the book is uncapped (§169: naming is free, and entries land by themselves from counterparties, Safes and the four devnet signers), so a book of three hundred at up to three services each, paced against one shared public host, turns a scroll to the bottom into minutes of chain reads nobody asked for. `AddressNames` persists answers **including misses** (most addresses have set no name anywhere, so the unkept miss is the expensive case) and re-asks after a fortnight.

**WHAT IS NOT BUILT, and it is a measurement rather than a shrug.** The user asked for "the ENS they HOLD", and holding is not the same fact as the primary name. `balanceOf` answers — `0x1c0a…5a20` holds **79** `.wei` names — but **neither contract is `ERC721Enumerable`**: `tokenOfOwnerByIndex` and `totalSupply` both revert, so the ids cannot be walked on-chain and listing them needs an indexer (Alchemy credits against a shared-key ceiling, for an uncapped book). The name IS recoverable from an id without one — `tokenURI` returns a data URI whose base64 JSON is `{"name":"vitalik.wei",…}` — so this is the second half of the problem, not the first. `WeiNamesSource.heldCount` exists and is reported by the probe; no surface draws it yet, and 79 chips in a book row would be the wrong reading anyway.

**Also declined**: forward and reverse are independent on all three services (`alice.gwei` resolves to an address whose primary is unset), so a blank row means "set no primary name", never "owns nothing" — no copy anywhere says otherwise.

**GUARDED.** `scripts/wei-names-selftest.sh` compiles `WeiNames.swift` and `Keccak256.swift` WHOLE and unmodified — ~45 assertions against the measured fixtures, 10 mutations, and drift guards for the forward verification, the family order, the demo gate on all three reads, the six call sites not regrowing their ternary, `canServe`'s ENS-exactly form, the §169 no-write rule and the address staying first in the reach list; negative guards read a comment-stripped copy, since both files document these rules by naming what they must not do (the Obsidian/Cursor lesson). **The harness found three defects in its own subject before this landed**: the dead sort above, a vacuous ambiguity check, and a redundant `length > 0` beside a `!text.isEmpty` that already covered it — two conditions guarding one thing, where only one can be shown to work. `live-integrations.sh` carries the drift class no local harness can see, and it is the §311 shape: when a registry stops answering the app does not break, it goes QUIET — every row draws, no name appears, and from outside that is indistinguishable from "this address set no name".

**UNSEEN ON A DEVICE.** Every changed file parses, the harness is green and the reach audit passes; no simulator was opened (standing rule) and no full `verify.sh` has run. The one thing genuinely unmeasured is the app's own path end to end: the contracts were measured directly and the Swift encoders were fired at them from a scratch binary, but no book row or card has drawn a `.wei` name on a screen.

## 599. Surprise and delight in the address book, and the two proposals that were already built (user: "how would you add surprise and delight to the address book", then "do all", 2026-09-04)

Five moments were proposed. **Two of them already existed and a third aimed at dead code** — which is §418's lesson arriving for the fourth time in this file, and the reason it is recorded before anything else: *read the room's most recent ledger entry before proposing against it, because the code will not tell you which of its gaps were deliberate.*

- **"First crossed paths — a dateline from the oldest landed transfer"** is `AddressSpine.Root.appeared(at:walletName:)`, shipped with §446, printing the date plus the word "First" plus which wallet it turned up in. Building it again would have been a second answer to one question.
- **"Copy gather — the address chunks gather toward the copy button"** aimed at `AddressCard.addressBlock`, which is **dead code**: §499's reach section replaced it and nothing has referenced `addressBlock` or `copyPill` since. The moment it asked for is also already there — §502 gave copying a sweep through the characters that were taken and an unfold of the house short form into the whole address. Two copy answers on one screen is exactly the drift this codebase folds together, so the item is void rather than rebuilt. (`AddressChunkFlow`, `addressChunkReveal` and `AddressSpine.revealRank` are alive only through those two dead properties; they are left standing and named here rather than removed in a delight pass.)
- **"First-ink — the first address you name by hand gets a stroke wipe"** was decoration with no fact behind it, and this room's own bar rules it out: each of §441's five moments is tied to something that really happened (a star really moved the wallet, a connection really is new). Nothing about an identicon changes when you name it — `WalletFace` derives from the address. What naming really changes is recorded below.

### 1. A reverse record is a CLAIM, and ENS was believing it

Not delight at all; found while asking whether a "round-trip verified" seal was worth drawing. **`WeiNamesSource.primaryName` has forward-verified since §597 and its own doc says ENS is owed the same check — and this app did not make it.** `ENS.reverseName` took `name` off `api.ensideas.com` and handed it straight to a book row, so a stranger's address could stand in our own chrome as `vitalik.eth` beside somebody's money. Anybody can point a reverse record at any name; ENSIP-3 requires the forward resolution to come back to the same address before the name is believed.

**Measured 2026-09-04, and the measurement is why the check is OURS**: that endpoint answers the forward and the reverse query with one byte-identical object, so its response cannot say whether it verified. It is a third party's undocumented internals, and this is the one claim on the screen that must not rest on them. `NameResolve.forwardVerified` costs one request, is spent ONLY on a non-empty answer (the rare case — most addresses have set no primary name), fails CLOSED, and compares case-insensitively because EIP-55 puts a checksum in the case of a hex address's letters.

**So the seal is not drawn, and that is the better answer.** All three services now meet one bar, which means every name the book shows is verified and a badge saying so would be a badge on every row — a mark that says nothing, which is what §498 took off these faces a week ago. The honest form of "show that it round-trips" is *never show one that doesn't*.

### 2. The address introduces itself (`AddressArrivingName`)

§597 taught the card to stand an auto name under the name the ADDRESS claims and drew the swap as a cross-fade — the treatment this app uses for a value that CHANGED. Nothing changed: the app asked three registries who this is, one answered, and the answer arrived while you were looking. So it is **written in**, character by character. A typewriter is the one motion that says a name was *received* rather than recomputed, and it is honest in a way a flourish is not — the characters appear in the order the string has them, and the string is the whole of what arrived.

Three rules carry it. **It runs only on an ARRIVAL**: the card's `.task` reads what is already known before it asks, so a second visit draws the name on the first frame and types nothing, which is right because nothing was learned. **It holds the STRING, not a flag** — `nameField`'s text is rebuilt by `.id(shownName)` on any later rename too, so a flag would type back a name you had just typed yourself, which is the app performing your own act. **The caret is what stops it reading as a glitch**: from the first frame there is a mark on the line, so the name grows out of something rather than out of a blank, and it does not blink (a repeating animation is a loading state — `AddressCopySweep`'s rule). The clock is fixed and the STEP absorbs the length, so a forty-character subdomain lands on the same beat as `a.wei`. Reduce Motion draws the whole name; VoiceOver always reads the whole name, because a prefix is a different name and on this screen that matters more than anywhere in the app.

The existing scale swap is kept and the two run together: the placeholder is carried out while the name types over the space it left.

### 3. The same arrival, said where it changes what you can do

The reach list GROWS while you read it — the names land asynchronously — and the row used to appear between two frames. It now enters on the `withAnimation` the card's own task already wrapped `primaryNames` in. The transition is declared on the row and the animation is NOT: this list must not animate its own rebuild, or the address row would scale every time §502's copy unfold redraws it.

### 4. What naming actually changes, on the card that has nothing landed

§441 built the retitle cascade so a new name can be watched sweeping down every landed transfer — and §462 says the common card is a young one with nothing landed, where the cascade has nothing to sweep. Two things really change there and both were drawn as values snapping:

- **The pencil retires.** It is on the card because naming is the thing to do, so the moment it is done the mark has nothing left to ask for. It leaves as an object now, the way the star flight and the kind turn-over leave.
- **The empty-spine sentence adopts the name** ("Transfers with *Mum* land here as they arrive") — the only place a young card visibly learns it. A cross-fade and not the typewriter, for §2's reason: this is a sentence taking a word you supplied, not a name arriving from elsewhere.
- **"Not kept" retires** when naming puts an address in the book. `isInBook` flips in the same beat the title changes — a real transition between two things the card says about one address, previously a word disappearing.

**UNSEEN ON A DEVICE.** The iOS build is green and every changed file parses; no simulator was opened (standing rule) and no full `verify.sh` has run. Every moment here is a motion, so none of them is provable by any static check in this repo — the typewriter's clock, the caret's height at Dynamic Type sizes, and whether the arrival reads as one moment or two are device questions. The ENS verification is the one change with a testable consequence and it has not been exercised against a live resolver from the app.

## 600. The source room's list is bounded and its head is not (user: "how would you optimize the app. feels laggy on load and also swiping between screens", then "do all of what you suggest and recommend", 2026-09-04)

Third report of this symptom pair in fifteen days, after the passes recorded in `docs/perf-swipe-and-rise-spec.md` (2026-08-21) and `docs/perf-spec.md` (2026-09-01). **The fact that decides everything here: no number has ever been taken on a phone in Release.** Every measurement in this project's perf record is Debug on a simulator, so a report arriving three days after a green pass has two readings — the fixes landed and the lag is something no instrument spans, or the fixes landed and the phone is not the simulator — and nothing on this machine can tell them apart. The full plan, the mechanism table and the decision table live in `docs/perf-load-and-swipe-spec.md`; this entry records the rulings and the four changes that did not need the phone first.

**THE RULING: a source room's LIST may be bounded while its HEAD reads the whole room.** The 2026-08-14 ruling refused a permanent `fetchLimit` there, and it was right about what it was refusing: `sourceHead` composed from `visible`, so a bound made `XRoom`'s "your loudest year" describe the newest N posts — §83 fake status in the room whose entire promise is that it holds your history. But that is an argument about the HEAD, not about the list. Nothing on screen ever shows more than `windowRowBudget` rows. So the two readers are separated rather than the bound refused: the `@Query` carries `sourceRoomFetchLimit` (600, twenty "Show older" windows), and `recomputeHeads` makes its own unbounded, predicated, unprojected fetch through `FeedScreen.fullRoomRows`. The head still sees every row it ever saw.

**It is strictly less work, not a trade.** The head's full read runs inside `.task(id: headKey)` and is memoised in `headMemo` — once per (room, corpus revision). The `@Query` it replaces was read on every body pass: several per swipe, and once per bridge save through a foreground burst, each one materialising a bulk-import room's thousands of rows **with** the heavy inline text that branch has been obliged to carry since 2026-08-31. What changes is when the work happens, which is this project's own standing test for whether a perf change is structural.

**Three consequences that would each have been silent, and are handled.** (1) `reachedFetchCeiling` covers source rooms now — left All-only, the footer would have read "That's everything from X" over a room holding ten thousand posts, which is the §83 failure the property exists to prevent, committed by the change that was careful about §83 everywhere else. (2) The per-source `@Query`-staleness net compares `min(rawCount, sourceRoomFetchLimit)` against `things.count`: uncapped, every room past the ceiling is a PERMANENT mismatch, so the unbounded recovery fetch would run on every foreground of every bulk-import room — the exact cost this removes, arriving through the safety net instead of through the list, with the room rendering perfectly throughout. That is the All room's own 2026-08-06 correction, owed here the moment this room gained a bound. (3) `fullRoomRows` returns its fallback whenever the fetch comes back SHORTER than the list already has, because §592's report is that `$0.source == source` can disagree with a plain fetch on the same store — so the worst case is a head over the bounded list, which is the pre-§600 behaviour, rather than a head over nothing, which would silently delete every reading in the room.

**The row entrance stands down during a swipe.** A room change is a remount (§265), so every swipe played `RowEntrance` on its first thirteen rows — thirteen animation transactions, each with its own delay — inside the frames the page's own move transition needed. It is also a design point rather than only a cost: the row is already arriving, carried by the page it sits on, and lifting it again on top of that is the second animation on one moment that the modifier's own rule ("one animation per moment") forbids. Suppressed only while `rowBudget` is set, so a scroll into a new row and a room entered from a chip tap while standing still both keep it. Twenty hand-spelled call sites became one `rowEntrance(_:)` helper first — otherwise the flag would have been twenty identical edits and twenty places for the next one to drift. Reduce Motion is checked BESIDE the new flag, never replaced by it, or §299's accessibility gap returns.

**`SwipeClock` reports in Release now, and that is the item the whole spec turns on.** It was `#if DEBUG` from the day it shipped, which made the one instrument built for the one reported symptom structurally unable to say anything about the configuration people run — while the pass that built it closed by saying a device trace is the reading that would settle it. Gated at runtime on `-swipeTimer YES` instead, which is `LaunchClock.reports`' and `SweepClock.isOn`' own shape; a shipped build passes the flag to nobody. Its new `span(_:_:)` times one synchronous block off the swipe trace, and `MainSurface.computedChips` uses it on `newestPerSource()` — the walk measured at ~640 of 4,300 cold-launch samples on 2026-08-11, which `#Index` was added to make cheaper on 2026-09-01 and which **nothing has re-read since, on either configuration**. `LaunchPerf.time` could not answer it: that whole file is `#if DEBUG`. **Do not persist the chip strip's order until that line has been read** — the fix is only worth its cost if the walk is still expensive, and a strip that reshuffles on every launch is worse than a slower one.

**Two audits refused the change until it was finished, both correctly.** `fetch-bound-audit.py` flagged `fullRoomRows` as an unbounded fetch — it is, by design, and it is now in `KNOWN_UNBOUNDED` with the reason — and in the same run reported that the `init` exemption it used to carry now **matches nothing**, because the fetch that exemption defended is the one this ruling bounded. An exemption nothing can reach is a check satisfied for the wrong reason, so it is removed rather than left. `prd-index-audit.py` refused every citation of this section until this entry existed.

**Guarded by `room-perf-selftest.sh` section D** — 61 checks and 27 mutations, all proven to fail. Two of its existing checks and two of its existing mutations were AMENDED rather than deleted: the head's `.live` filter moved into `fullRoomRows` with the read it guards (a guarded function that moves takes its guard with it), and the instrument check is INVERTED the way §586a's fade assertion was — it demanded that every `NSLog` sit under `#if DEBUG`, which is precisely what made the phone unmeasurable, so it now demands a runtime gate instead. A stale mutation is worse than none: it matches nothing, survives every run, and reports a rule as proven that it never tested.

**WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT, and each is gated on a measurement rather than parked.** Snapshotting the outgoing room during a slide (two live `@Query`s mid-transition) waits on the `sample` A/B that would say whether it matters — proposing it without one is the "plausible fix before the cheap instrument" mistake this project has a standing rule against, and it has now been deferred on that ground three times. Freezing the bottom bar's glass backdrop during a transition waits on an Instruments hitches trace, because it is a design change and no main-thread instrument here can see a GPU cost. Persisting the chip order waits on the `span` line above. Moving head composition off the main actor waits on a value projection of the row, which is the same projection that would end the SwiftData liveness class and is its own pass.

**UNMEASURED, and that is the honest grade for every number in this entry.** The build is green on both platforms, the guard is green, and not one frame of any of it has been observed on a device. `docs/perf-load-and-swipe-spec.md` Phase 0 is the reading that would change that, and it needs the phone.

## 598. The Privacy devnet's ring, its plain words, its own moments (user: "how else would you improve the Privacy devnet UI", then "and also add surprise and delight", then "can you make sure we are not hand rolling anything either and are using components from the other wallet and devnet rooms", 2026-09-04)

§596 made the room BEHAVE like the family. This pass is about what it SAYS, what it DRAWS, and the fact that it had never once marked anything.

**1. THE CHIPS SPOKE A DIFFERENT LANGUAGE FROM THE ROOM.** Two of the seven read "Nullifiers" and "Roots" while the lede, every scope headline, every row's meta line, both sheets and both accessibility labels said **spend keys** and **snapshots** — so the room taught one vocabulary everywhere except in the one place a person meets it FIRST. A strip is a table of contents, and a table of contents in a private dialect sends somebody looking for the thing they already understand. The chips are "Spend keys" and "Snapshots" now. **The case names and raw values do NOT move** and that is load-bearing: they are the persisted pick (`chrome.privacyDevnetSection`) and the deep link's own word, so renaming them would silently reset every stored scope and break a saved link. The jargon survives where it earns its place — the move sheet still says nullifier beside the keys it explains, which is where a reader has the object in front of them.

**2. THE WINDOW IS A RING IN THE CHAIN'S OWN BYTECODE, SO IT IS DRAWN AS ONE.** EIP-8272's predeploy masks a slot with `0x1fff` and `PrivacyDevnetRoots.ringIndex` already computed the wrap — and the room drew a straight 4pt bar that needed a caption at each end to say which way time ran ("leaves the chain's memory" … "now"), printed on Home AND again under every lane in the Roots scope. **`PrivacyDevnetRing` needs neither: the gap at the bottom IS the exit**, so a snapshot that leaves the window falls into it, and the shape carries what the caption was carrying. NOW at the top, age clockwise, the direction a clock face already teaches. The lane stack is deleted with it — `PrivacyDevnetFigure.lanes`, `laneCap` and `PrivacyDevnetTrack` are gone, and one ring carries every source's references.

**3. SLOTS ARE NOT A UNIT ANYBODY CAN FEEL, AND THIS AMENDS §593d IN ONE NARROW PLACE.** That entry put the seconds conversion at the bottom of the roots list, once, about the window rather than about anybody's proof, reasoning that a per-row countdown in minutes is one assumption repeated as a fact. **That reasoning holds for a row in a list and does not hold for the crown**: the headline read "for another 4,096 slots" — a measurement nobody outside this devnet can size, in the largest type on the card. A number a reader cannot feel is not a more honest number, it is an unread one. So `PrivacyDevnetRoots.approximate` leads wherever the clock is drawn, under three rules that keep it inside §83: it always says **"about"**; the **measured slot count travels beside it** so nothing observed is replaced by anything assumed; and the assumption is still named out loud once per surface by `windowNote`, unchanged. The rungs are coarse on purpose — "about 11 hours", never "about 11.4", because the extra digit is the part somebody would act on.

**4. THE LEDE STATES THE STATE; THE RING STATES THE CLOCK.** The head sentence carried both facts and now carries one. `remaining` stays on the `Lede.rootLive` case rather than being dropped: it is what RANKS the leading reference in `head`, and the reference the head chose is the one the ring's own reading is taken from — so the sentence and the number inside the ring can never describe two different snapshots.

**5. A 32-BYTE SOURCE ID NAMES NOTHING.** The Roots scope labelled each lane `0x1f4a20b8…3c91` in an 84pt mono column, which is not an identity a reader can hold across a figure, a row and a sheet. Sets wear ORDINALS now — the ring's marks, the room's rows (as `WalletRowMark.monogram`, so the figure and the list are one identity) and the move sheet all carry the same number, off `bySource`'s already-total order so it cannot renumber between opens. **One set is not "Set 1"**: an ordinal implies a second, so a single source says "The set". The bytes stay as the row's subtitle, where an identifier belongs. **The collapse changed with it** — marks fold by (set, slot) rather than by slot, because two sources may register in the same slot and folding those draws two anonymity sets as one point, which is the error the ring exists to make visible.

## The moments this room had never had

Frames fires "Your first transaction landed"; Hegotá and vibenet flash their own writes. **This seat had not one `chrome.flash` and not one first-sight animation** — in the room whose subject is the rarest thing on any of the four chains. It read as a very careful instrument that never once said "look at this". `Model/PrivacyDevnetMoments.swift` is Foundation-only with every store injectable, because a once-ever flag whose only proof is "it did not fire again on my phone" is not proven at all.

**Three rules every moment is held to.** (1) **NEVER RETROACTIVE** — one `isFirstRead` flag seeds every moment in silence on an install's first completed sweep, because firing "your first" over a week-old account is the §83 claim in its most personal form. (2) **NEVER A CELEBRATION OF SOMEBODY ELSE'S ACT** — this chain's pool is an application contract whose ABI this project does not have (§593), so **this phone can never spend a one-time key**, and every nullifier the room will ever show belongs to a stranger. The pool moment is therefore worded as a DISCOVERY and claims no authorship. (3) **SILENT WHERE SILENCE IS THE ANSWER** — a snapshot leaving the window is drawn and never announced, because §593 ruled nothing is lost when it goes and nothing can be done before it does.

**The first settle rides the NONCE, which is the only signal this seat has.** Frames watches a pending row become a landed one; this seat keeps no pending list, and building one to carry a toast would be a machine larger than the moment. The nonce is incremented by the chain on INCLUSION, so 0 → non-zero is exactly "a transaction this phone signed turned out to be real", read from the same `eth_getTransactionCount` the room already makes — free when the key's address is watched, one extra request when it is not, and asked at all only while the moment is owed, so it stops happening the day it fires.

**THE SWEEP IS TOLD THIS PHONE'S ADDRESS AND NEVER LOOKS IT UP, and that is a guard working rather than a guard bent.** `privacy-selftest.sh` fails the build if `PrivacyDevnetBridge` so much as NAMES `PrivacyDevnetKey` — that file is what every room open drives, on a timer, with no tap behind it. Reading a public address signs nothing, and the guard is deliberately coarse; **weakening it to let one convenience through is how a coarse guard becomes no guard**. So the view that already knows publishes it, and a sweep that runs before anything mounted simply has no address, which costs nothing because the moment needs somebody looking at the room anyway.

**The ring is alive, and the clamp is the whole safety argument.** The head slot is read once every two minutes and the window drains continuously, so a ring that only moves when a sweep lands is a clock that ticks twice an hour. `PrivacyDevnetFigure.drifted` moves each mark between sweeps — and **may never carry one to the rim**: only a real read may say a snapshot has aged out, which is right twice over, because the seconds-per-slot figure is this devnet's assumed cadence and the aged state is the only one on this ring that changes what a row SAYS. Past `driftCap` it **freezes** rather than running on, since extrapolating an unobserved hour is inventing an hour of chain. A mark that really does age out then travels to the gap and hollows rather than teleporting there — the one place this room has to show a thing ending.

**A spend key seals itself the first time this device sees it.** The ring's hole IS its claim, and the room drew that claim already finished for every key it had ever shown. `PrivacyDevnetMoments.unseen` turns the animation on for genuinely new keys alone, and it seeds silently on an install's first read — otherwise somebody's first open seals forty rings at once, which is a room celebrating its own contents. The ledger is `UserDefaults` and not a `Thing`: "have you looked at this" is a fact about THIS DEVICE'S SCREEN (`AddressConnectionsSeen`'s ruling), so **no new field and no CloudKit deploy**.

**Declined, with reasons.** A sponsored-transaction moment — no measured transaction on this chain has a payer differing from its sender, so it would never fire. Any wording implying concealment — nothing on this chain hides the sender, and a celebration is the worst place to blur that (§593).

## The components it was not using

Asked directly whether anything was hand-rolled, the answer was measured rather than assumed: **Frames' sheets, one chip away, use `DSSpecRow` ten times and `DSStamp` six; this seat's sheets used neither.** It hand-rolled the move sheet's tail facts as a `VStack` of tertiary sentences carrying their labels inside the value ("From 0x1f…", "Block 13347") — which is the shape `DSSpecTable` exists for, because it was written three times at three column widths before anyone noticed. Its key rows were an `HStack` with a hand-placed trailing word, which is `WalletRow`'s terminal form plus `DSStamp` spelled out — and `DSStamp` exists because that word was drawn twice at two weights. Both are converted; `.quiet` is not a shrug but this room's own no-colour-for-state ruling. **And the seat had TWO hex shorteners** — `PrivacyDevnetRoomCard.shortHex` over `Data` and a private `shortHash` over `String` — eliding at different lengths, so a key and the transaction that spent it were cut differently on the same sheet. One spelling now, in `PrivacyDevnetName`; `WalletStore.shortAddress` is deliberately not reused, because an address is checksummed and shortened for recognition while these are opaque hashes shortened for width.

**Two near-duplicates were examined and left alone, which is the other half of the answer.** `PrivacyDevnetAnatomy` and `HegotaFrameStrip` look like one component and encode different things — Hegotá draws one continuous bar whose segments are MODES weighted by gas USED, this draws separate shapes weighted by BUDGET plus keys, snapshots and a payer pill, and §596 made that shape vocabulary the room's own. Merging them would need Hegotá's mode labels to survive a type they do not share. `PrivacyDevnetMore` has no shared equivalent anywhere (Hegotá spells its overflow line inline), so it stays this seat's.

**Guarded**: `privacy-selftest.sh` compiles `PrivacyDevnetMoments` whole beside the other four, at **38 mutations and 25 drift guards** — the ring's geometry, the nudge, the exit sweep, the drift clamp and freeze, the ordinals, the hedge, both moments' seeding, the seen cap, plus drift guards that the track cannot return, the caption cannot return, the sheets keep using the shared components, and there is only one hex shortener. **Two of its own defects are the reason this repo demands mutation proof.** The exit-sweep fixture crowded three marks at NOW, where they nudge to 0/12/24 and never approach the arc's end — so deleting the sweep left the suite green and **the mutation SURVIVED**; the case that can fail crowds them at the OLD end, where the push runs them into the gap and draws three live snapshots as three that have left. And the lede guard fired against the FIXED source, because the comment above it quotes the sentence it replaced — the comment-stripped-copy lesson, earned again.

**UNSEEN ON A DEVICE.** iOS builds green and all 38 mutations are caught; no simulator was opened (standing rule). The ring, the seal and the drift were mocked in `prototype/privacy-room-598-mock.html` for review instead. Three things are reasoned rather than seen: the arc's offset-then-rotate placement (the counter-rotation that keeps an ordinal upright), the `TimelineView` cadence at 6s, and whether a 128pt ring plus a four-line sentence still fits Home's 300pt slot — which is the measurement that has already been wrong twice in this room (§593b).

## 602. The Privacy room's false promise, its missing rows, its own account, and what a transaction actually cost (user: "how else would you improve the privacy room", then "do all", 2026-09-04)

Six items, and the first is the only one that was a lie rather than a gap.

**1. THE SEAT'S OWN CARD PROMISED SOMETHING THAT STOPPED BEING TRUE EIGHT BUILDS AGO.** Its connected-state `can:` line read *"This seat only ever reads — it makes no key, signs nothing and sends nothing"*, and §593d gave the room Create, Top up and Send. The comment directly above that line states the rule it broke: the promise and the catalog's copy "retire together, never one without the other". The catalog half was retired AND guarded the day sending landed; this half was left standing, on the one surface whose whole job is saying what a seat can do, in the room whose whole subject is what can and cannot be claimed. It is worded as its two siblings word it now, because it is the same fact about the same kind of key on the same fork — and the plain-scalar clause earns its place here more than anywhere, since this is the card somebody reads while deciding whether a privacy devnet is safe to try. **Both halves are guarded now**, which is what that comment always said the rule was.

**2. HOME PROMISED "THE LAST FEW MOVES" AND SHOWED NONE.** `homeMoves` budgeted rows against `DSRoomSlot`'s fixed 300pt box because Home drew them INSIDE the slot — and that box clips. Two estimates in a row (154, then 232) each left one row that fitted the arithmetic and was cut mid-line on a device, reported twice with a screenshot, and §593b's answer was to draw NO moves whenever the window figure was present. Which is every time a proof is live, i.e. whenever the room has anything to say. **The rows are below the rail now**, where `PrivacyDevnetRoomList` draws every other scope's and where nothing clips — the §593d split finally applied to the one scope exempt from it. So there is no box to budget against and no third estimate to get wrong: `homeMoveCap` is a stated three, and "a few is three" keeps its own reason (past three this becomes the Activity scope one chip away). The Foundation file's hand-mirrored copy of `DSRoomChassis.visualSlot` is deleted with the budget that needed it, rather than left to drift.

**3. THE KEY'S OWN ACCOUNT HAD NO SEAT IN THE ROOM THAT MADE IT.** Creating a key did not watch its address, and every reading this room has is per watched address — so after Create and Top up, the balance you had just claimed appeared in no roster row, no rail seat, no tally and no face, unless you thought to paste your own address into the field on a screen you reach by leaving. Watching is a READ (§593's own word), so this adds no capability the tap did not already grant; it makes the account the tap just created visible. It also makes §598's first-settle nonce read free, since the sweep now reads that address anyway. `PrivacyDevnetName.of` answers **"This phone"** for it — vibenet's own word — because a watched address with no name reads as a stranger's hex, which is the wrong thing to call the account the app itself generated.

**4. THE ROOM COULD SAY WHAT EVERY TRANSACTION WAS ALLOWED AND WHAT NONE OF THEM COST.** No per-frame breakdown is served on this chain (measured, §593a), which is why `Frame.gasUsed` is permanently nil — and the walk was ALSO throwing away the transaction-level total, off a receipt it had already fetched for the payer. The receipt's `rc` was bound inside its own chained `if`, so a real number the chain reported and this app already held in memory was unreachable to everything downstream. **Zero extra requests**: bound once, read twice. `PrivacyDevnetFigure.allowance` sums the frame budgets **all-or-nothing** (`shares`' own rule, and the worst kind of invented number to get wrong — "used 21,000 of 30,000" reads as measured on both sides), returns nil for a transfer that has no frames rather than a zero it could overspend, and refuses a sum wide enough to overflow rather than wrapping it into a small honest-looking figure. The strip's full width IS the allowance, so `usedShare` draws as a thin track BENEATH the frame bars on that same axis — under them, never behind them, because a fill inside the segments would read as the per-frame breakdown this chain does not serve. **Clamped at 1, and the clamp is a real case**: the receipt covers the whole transaction while the allowance sums only the frames, so an intrinsic cost outside any frame pushes the ratio past 1, and the exact figures are stated in words beside it where an overrun can be read honestly.

**5. THE STANDING CEILING WAS PRINTED THREE TIMES ON ONE SCREEN.** All three walk sentences drew under every list that had rows — Activity, Frames and Sponsors — so the room's own explanation of itself appeared three times in its quietest ink, which is §315's fine-print failure wearing a room head's clothes. They were never one kind of fact, and that is what decides where each goes: **the floor is how this room works and is true forever**, so it is said once, on Home, under the acts; **the two cuts are what happened on this pass**, so they stay with the rows they truncated, and they already draw only when they really bit (on every measured pass so far, never).

## And then somebody looked at it

**Six passes from §593 to §598 and not one screenshot** — every one of them ending "UNSEEN on a device". The room was opened on a simulator for this entry, and it found two defects no static check could have:

- **The ring sat against the leading edge with the whole right half of the card empty** and ~200pt of dead air between it and the rail. A `VStack` hugs its top and a trailing `Spacer` pins its content left, so the room's lead figure was a small object in a large blank card — the "tiny and top justified" defect §588 fixed for Frames and §596 fixed for this room's other figures, arriving a third time in a shape neither of those fixes covered. Centred, given the leftover height, and grown to 156.
- **"about 14 hours" wrapped to two lines inside the ring** and read as a second headline under the first. It is the ring's caption, not its lede: one line, scaled down before it wraps. The rim went 4pt → 5pt for the same reason — the straight track it replaced was 4pt across the full card and read clearly, and the same weight bent into a circle all but disappeared on a dark ground, so the ring's own shape was the hardest thing to see on the card it leads.
- **Two spellings of one number on one sheet**: the step budgets printed `320000` while the Gas row two blocks below printed `21,000`. The second spelling arrived with this pass, which is exactly how that drift always arrives; one `grouped` helper now, and these are quantities somebody reads rather than the hex the chain speaks.

**`WalletStore.shortAddress`'s tail-only form was checked and left alone** — "From …f980" looks like a truncation bug and is the app's own documented ruling with its own harness. Read the ruling before fixing what looks broken.

**Guarded**: 42 mutations and 30 drift guards in `privacy-selftest.sh`. **Its own first run found a redundant guard rather than a bug**: `allowance` carried an empty-list check AND a zero test, so the mutation against the first SURVIVED — two guards for one case means neither can be shown to matter, so the second one went rather than the test being made cleverer. What remains is that the zero test alone stands between a plain transfer and a denominator of zero.

**What is still unseen**: the used bar has never drawn. The demo's moves carry no `gasUsed` and inventing one would be a fabricated fixture in a file whose own rule is that every hex value was read back off the chain, so the arithmetic is proven by the harness and the drawing by nothing. The two `chrome.flash` moments from §598 are likewise unfired — both need a chain event no simulator can produce.

## 604. The screenshots in a connected folder never became screenshots, and iCloud was never the reason (user: "screenshots in my files folder are still not showing as screenshots", 2026-09-04)

Reported twice. The second time is the interesting one, because the first fix had already shipped and changed nothing.

**The room drew a wall of filenames.** Thirty CleanShot PNGs in a connected folder, each row its raw file name, no thumbnail, no tile — the §283 failure the Files room's mixed shape exists to prevent, in the room built to prevent it.

**A file in a picked folder is readable only inside an active `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource` window on that folder.** Outside one the read is REFUSED — and refused is indistinguishable from *the bytes are not here yet*: `CGImageSourceCreateWithURL` returns nil either way, so `thumbnail` gives no pixels, `ocrRead` reports `attempted == false`, `ocrAt` is correctly left nil, and the very same file is re-read and re-fails on every foreground pass for the life of the install. No error, no log line, nothing on any screen. The grid needs pixels to admit a row, so no tile; the retitle only fires when OCR reads something, so every title stays the file name. One cause, all three symptoms.

**It was a refactor, and it had been true for five weeks.** The scope used to be opened at the top of `FilesIngest.heal` and covered the whole read loop. On 2026-07-29 the walk moved into its own detached task to stop reconstructing paths from strings — a good change — and the scope went WITH the walk, so from that commit it closed the moment the walk returned. The §283 grid shipped four days later, on top of it. A connected folder's images have therefore arguably never healed on a real device.

**Three things hid it, and the asymmetry points the wrong way.** A folder's VIDEO still tiles, because `ImportMedia.posterFrame` opens the scope itself. A text file still shows its preview, because `preview(of:)` is called from inside `refresh`'s own scoped task. So the one read that broke was the one read with no scope of its own — and everything around it looked healthy. Nothing here could see it either: on the simulator a picked folder is usually in-sandbox, `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource` returns false, and the reads succeed anyway, which is why every check in this repo passed over it for five weeks.

**The first fix read the symptom as iCloud eviction (2026-09-03) and was wrong.** An evicted iCloud file genuinely does need `startDownloadingUbiquitousItem`, that request is still made and still right, and it was never the cause. The generalisable half: *a read that fails permissionlessly and a read that fails for want of bytes look identical at the call site*, so when both are possible, rule out the one you control before instrumenting the one you do not.

**The ruling: the scope belongs to the READ, never to whichever caller happens to enclose it.** `thumbnail` and `ocrRead` take the folder and open their own window, which is `posterFrame`'s own contract — and precisely why that one survived the refactor that broke these two. Nested starts are refcounted, so a reader is safe alongside any window a caller has already opened, and a future refactor cannot separate a read from its permission because they are now the same function.

**Guarded** by `scripts/files-scope-selftest.sh` (in `verify.sh`), and the guard reads ONE FUNCTION'S BODY rather than the file: this file opens a scope in three other places (the walk, the audio handle, the poster frame), so a file-level grep passes vacuously — it is exactly the check that would have called the broken tree clean. Four mutations, each a single-line deletion of the thing the check names: either reader dropping its scope, a reader leaking one, and a call site dropping the folder. The second exists because a sibling still being correct is how a loose grep scores a broken tree green.

**Still unproven on a device.** The scope's closure is demonstrable in the source and the symptom set matches it exactly and asymmetrically, but no read has been watched succeeding on a real picked folder from this host. The tell that it worked will be titles: a CleanShot name is in `isMachineGeneratedName`, so a healed row stops saying `CleanShot 2026-09-04 at 18.17.43@2x.png` and starts saying what the picture says.

## 605. The devnet sheets say less — one fact, one place, across three rooms (user: "i want the devnet rooms to be super tidy and very polished. the thing sheets for example on privacy room seem like a lot of words are they or is it just me? please also check hegot and frames. these need to be world class", 2026-09-04)

It was not just them.
